screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use when building and auditing Solidity contracts. First, you will understand and apply Solidity's inheritance syntax and mechanics to create modular, reusable contracts that reduce duplication and clarify intent. Third, you will be able to design abstract contracts and interfaces: decide when to provide partial implementations and when to declare only signatures for interoperability. Fourth, you will explain how multiple inheritance is resolved through C3 Linearization, so you can predict which base implementation takes precedence and avoid surprising behavior. Each objective pairs a conceptual understanding with a competency milestone: build a small derived contract, modify a virtual function, implement an abstract function, and reason about ordering in a multi-base scenario. These skills will make your smart contracts easier to maintain and safer to extend. Keep an eye out for common pitfalls: missing virtual keywords, incorrect override lists, and overly deep inheritance hierarchies that complicate audits.

screens.title: What is inheritance in Solidity?
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance in Solidity is the mechanism by which one contract acquires the state variables and functions of another, enabling reuse and modular design. A contract that inherits is called the derived or child contract, and the contract being inherited from is the base or parent. When you declare contract Child is Parent, Child gains access to Parent’s public and internal members, which means you do not need to repeat common code like ownership checks, utility functions, or shared storage. A practical example is an Ownable base contract that stores the owner address and provides an onlyOwner modifier; derived contracts can use the modifier to protect sensitive functions without reimplementing the ownership check. One important detail is visibility: private members are not inherited, while internal and public are. Internal is useful for helper functions that should be visible to children but not exposed externally. Another nuance is constructors: if your base contract has initialization logic, derived contracts must ensure the base constructor is invoked either implicitly or via explicit parameters in the derived constructor. A common misconception is assuming inheritance copies code at deploy time; instead, the derived contract’s bytecode includes the selected behaviors, and explicit overrides determine which implementation is active. Think of inheritance as a design-time composition tool to centralize logic and make auditing easier when used with clear boundaries.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Inheritance lets a derived contract reuse public and internal members from a base contract, promoting modularity and centralized logic.

content.html:
Core Concept
Inheritance: base → derived

A derived contract gets public and internal members from its base contract. Use is to declare inheritance and rely on base implementations to centralize logic.

Visibility rules
Public and internal members are inherited. Private members are not.
Constructor behavior
Initialize base state either implicitly or by passing parameters in derived constructor.
Practical use
Centralize ownership, access control, or utility functions in bases to avoid duplication.
Key Takeaway

Treat inheritance as a controlled way to share state and behavior; keep bases focused and small.

Concrete example
// Example: Ownable base
contract Ownable {
  address public owner;
  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }
  modifier onlyOwner() { require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function"); _; }
}

// Derived contract uses onlyOwner without re-implementing it
contract MyContract is Ownable {
  function sensitiveAction() public onlyOwner { /* ... */ }
}
Common misconception
Inheritance copies code at runtime. In reality, derived contracts are compiled with selected implementations; explicit overrides decide active behavior.
Check your understanding
Why choose internal over private for a helper function you expect children to use?

screens.title: virtual and override keywords
screens.narratorSegment: The virtual and override keywords are Solidity’s explicit contract between base and derived contracts. Declaring a base function as virtual indicates that you intend it to be customizable by children. A derived contract that changes that function must mark its implementation with override. This pair enforces clarity: the compiler refuses accidental overrides and requires you to express intent. When multiple base contracts define the same signature, the derived override must list all affected bases in override(...). For example, if A and B both provide foo, and C inherits A and B, then a new implementation in C must include override(A, B) to compile. A common workflow is: mark base hooks that are intended to be specialized as virtual, implement default behavior in the base, then override in derived contracts and optionally call super to retain base logic. Using super. functionName lets you extend behavior rather than fully replace it. An example is a payment function that emits a log in the base and allows derived contracts to perform validations before calling super to preserve the event emission. A frequent pitfall is forgetting to mark the base function virtual; the compiler then prevents any derived override. Explicitness reduces surprise in deployed contracts where unintentional overrides could cause serious issues.

keyIdea.title: Override contract
keyIdea.text: virtual declares intent to allow change; override shows explicit modification and may list multiple bases when necessary.

content.html:
Definition
virtual & override

virtual marks base functions as customizable; override marks derived implementations and must list base contracts when multiple parents define the same function.

Step 1: Decide which base functions are hooks and mark them virtual.
Step 2: In derived contracts, use override to modify implementations.
Step 3: When combining multiple bases, list them inside override(...).
Misconception
You can safely override any function without compiler help. Solidity requires explicit virtual and override to prevent that problem.
Code walkthrough
// Base contract
function processPayment(address recipient, uint256 amount) public virtual returns (bool) {
  emit PaymentProcessed(recipient, amount, "Standard Payment");
  return true;
}

// Derived contract overrides
function processPayment(address recipient, uint256 amount) public override returns (bool) {
  require(amount >= subscriptionFee, "Amount too low for subscription");
  emit PaymentProcessed(recipient, amount, "Subscription Payment");
  return super.processPayment(recipient, amount);
}
Pro tip
Mark only those base functions you expect to vary; avoid making everything virtual by default.
Check
If the compiler errors about missing override, confirm the derived function lists all base names that declare the same signature.

screens.title: Using super to extend behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Calling the parent's implementation from an overriding function is a common pattern when you want to add checks or state updates while keeping base behavior intact. In Solidity you call super. functionName to invoke the next implementation in the inheritance chain as resolved by the compiler. A typical case is PaymentGateway with a processPayment function that emits an event and returns true. A SubscriptionPaymentGateway overrides processPayment to validate a subscription amount and then calls super. processPayment to retain the original emission and any shared accounting logic. This pattern reduces code duplication and ensures shared side effects, like event emission or bookkeeping, remain consistent across implementations. However, be mindful when multiple inheritance is present: super resolves according to C3 Linearization, so the exact parent invoked depends on the inheritance order. Another practical detail is ordering of side effects: perform validation first, then call super if validation passes, or call super first if you must perform a base action before derived behavior, but be explicit. A misconception is assuming super always calls the immediate parent; in multiple inheritance, super walks the linearized chain. When you rely on super, document why you call it and test the combined behavior thoroughly to avoid subtle surprises.

keyIdea.title: Extend, don't replace
keyIdea.text: Use super to keep base side effects and add validations or state updates in the derived implementation.

content.html:
Process Flow
Derived validation → super call
Pattern: perform derived-specific checks, update derived state, then call super to reuse the parent's shared logic such as event emission or bookkeeping.
Example sequence
  1. Derived contract validates input (e.g., subscription fee).
  2. Derived contract updates derived state (e.g., mark subscription active).
  3. Derived contract calls super to trigger shared side effects in base.
Common pitfall
Relying on super without understanding linearization can call an unexpected implementation when multiple bases are involved.
Code example
// Derived adds checks then calls super
function processPayment(address recipient, uint256 amount) public override returns (bool) {
  require(amount >= subscriptionFee, "Amount too low for subscription");
  // derived-specific updates here
  emit PaymentProcessed(recipient, amount, "Subscription Payment");
  return super.processPayment(recipient, amount);
}
Pro tip
Document why super is called and what state or events the base performs to avoid hidden side effects.
Check your understanding
If two bases emit the same event, which emission will run when you call super in the derived contract?

screens.title: Abstract contracts and interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Abstract contracts and interfaces both enforce structure but serve different design goals. An abstract contract can include implemented functions, state variables, and unimplemented functions marked as abstract; it cannot be deployed until its abstract functions are implemented by a derived contract. Use abstract contracts when you want to provide shared behavior or state but still force certain functions to be implemented by children. For example, an abstract PaymentProcessor might define a processPayment function signature without implementation while providing utility helpers to manage recipients. Interfaces are stricter: declared with the interface keyword, they contain only function signatures, cannot declare state or constructors, and are used to define public APIs that many contracts can adhere to. Choose an interface when you need a minimal, language-level guarantee about external calls and when you expect third-party contracts to implement the same signatures. A useful pattern is to code against interfaces for external interactions and inherit from abstract contracts for internal shared logic. A common misconception is thinking interfaces and abstract contracts are interchangeable; in practice interfaces are for external contracts and type checking, while abstract contracts are for partial implementations that supply shared code. Decide based on whether you need shared storage or only a signature contract.

keyIdea.title: Abstract vs Interface
keyIdea.text: Abstract contracts can carry state and partial implementations; interfaces are signature-only and enforce external API conformance.

content.html:
Abstract Contract
Partial implementation with required functions
Can include state, implemented helpers, and abstract functions that derived contracts must implement before deployment.
When to use
When you want to provide shared logic or storage but still force specialization through abstract functions.
Example role
Define a base workflow but leave one step for derived contracts to implement, such as a computation or policy decision.
Interface
Signature-only external API
Cannot have state or constructors. Use interfaces to define external behavior that many contracts conform to for interoperability.
When to use
When you need a contract to adhere to a specific set of externally callable functions with no shared storage.
Design tip
Reference interfaces in external calls to enable type checking and replaceable implementations.
Concrete contrast
State
Abstract: may have state. Interface: cannot.
Implementation
Abstract: may have code. Interface: no code.
Use case
Abstract: internal reuse. Interface: external contracts and typing.

screens.title: Multiple inheritance & C3 Linearization
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity supports multiple inheritance, which is powerful but demands discipline. When a contract inherits from multiple base contracts that define the same function signature, Solidity resolves which implementation is used using C3 Linearization, also described as method resolution order. The rule of thumb for Solidity is that the rightmost base in the is list has priority unless the derived contract explicitly overrides the function. For example, contract C is A, B will prefer B’s implementation of foo if both A and B implement it. If you need a different resolution or want to combine behavior, declare an override in C and call super to chain into the linearized sequence. A common mistake is assuming leftmost bases take precedence; developers should instead inspect the is ordering and add explicit override declarations to make intent clear. Very deep or diamond-shaped hierarchies make reasoning hard and increase audit surface area. Best practice is to keep the hierarchy shallow, document the expected linearization, and write unit tests that confirm which implementation runs for ambiguous functions. Also prefer explicit overrides that list parent contracts when you want to be very clear about which base implementations you are changing.

keyIdea.title: Method order
keyIdea.text: Solidity resolves multiple inheritance with C3 Linearization; rightmost bases have precedence unless overridden explicitly in the derived contract.

content.html:
Comparison
Left-first vs Right-first myth
Solidity chooses implementations based on a linearized order. The rightmost base in the is list is preferred unless the derived contract declares an override.
Example
contract C is A, B means B's foo will be used if A and B both have foo. To change that, add an override in C.
Pitfall
Diamond-shaped inheritance without explicit overrides can lead to subtle order-dependent behavior.
Practical checklist
  • Prefer shallow hierarchies to simplify linearization.
  • When in doubt, add an explicit override that lists parent contracts.
  • Write unit tests that assert which implementation executes for ambiguous functions.
Check

If functions with the same signature exist in multiple bases, confirm override lists and test the final behavior under your chosen is order.

screens.title: PaymentGateway → SubscriptionPaymentGateway
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough follows the PaymentGateway base and a SubscriptionPaymentGateway derived contract from the chapter. The base contract sets an owner and implements processPayment with basic behavior and an event emission. By declaring processPayment virtual, the base signals derived contracts can customize payment handling. The subscription gateway overrides processPayment to require a minimum subscription fee, perform subscription-specific updates, emit its own event, and then call super. processPayment so the base event and any common effects always occur. This structure allows the base to guarantee that certain bookkeeping runs on every payment, while derived contracts enforce their own policies. The example also shows adding an updateSubscriptionFee function protected by an onlyOwner modifier defined in the derived contract, demonstrating how access control and new functionality are layered on top of inherited behavior. When you implement this pattern, always test the sequence of events and state changes: verify the derived validation rejects insufficient amounts and that successful calls trigger both derived and base events. This combination of virtual, override, and super gives predictable extension points while preserving shared work. PaymentGateway → SubscriptionPaymentGateway means make base behavior guaranteed and allow derived contracts to validate or extend behavior before or after calling super.. In practical terms, a complete example of virtual, override, and super. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Worked example
keyIdea.text: Make base behavior guaranteed and allow derived contracts to validate or extend behavior before or after calling super.

content.html:
Example
PaymentGateway + Subscription override
// Base contract
contract PaymentGateway {
  address public owner;
  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }
  function processPayment(address _recipient, uint256 _amount) public virtual returns (bool) {
    emit PaymentProcessed(_recipient, _amount, "Standard Payment");
    return true;
  }
  event PaymentProcessed(address indexed recipient, uint256 amount, string paymentType);
}

// Derived contract
contract SubscriptionPaymentGateway is PaymentGateway {
  uint256 public subscriptionFee = 1 ether;
  function processPayment(address _recipient, uint256 _amount) public override returns (bool) {
    require(_amount >= subscriptionFee, "Amount too low for subscription");
    emit PaymentProcessed(_recipient, _amount, "Subscription Payment");
    return super.processPayment(_recipient, _amount);
  }
}
Explanation points
  • The base marks processPayment virtual so children can change behavior.
  • The derived contract enforces subscription-specific rules with require.
  • Calling super preserves the base event and shared side effects.
Scenario card
If subscriptionFee changes, only the derived contract needs to update it; base logic remains stable, reducing risk when modifying policies.
Key Takeaway

Use virtual + override + super to extend behavior safely while keeping core guarantees in the base.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: Ownable, Pausable, MyToken
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on activity in the chapter asks you to build small reusable base contracts and then compose them into a token. First, implement Ownable with an owner state and onlyOwner modifier. This centralizes access control logic so multiple derived contracts can reuse it. Next, create Pausable that inherits Ownable, adds a paused flag, pause and unpause functions protected by onlyOwner, and whenNotPaused and whenPaused modifiers to guard calls. Then write MyToken that inherits Pausable (which already inherits Ownable) and implements standard token state such as balances and a transfer function that uses whenNotPaused. This exercise reinforces several inheritance points: modifiers are inherited and applied without reimplementation; base constructors set up shared state like owner; and composed behavior means pausing is enforced across token transfers. When implementing, ensure modifiers check the correct flags and that pause/unpause logic can only be invoked by the owner. keyIdea.title: Lab objective
keyIdea.text: Compose small base contracts for access control and pausability, then inherit them to add guarded application logic like token transfers.

content.html:
Activity
Build Ownable, Pausable, and MyToken
// Ownable
contract Ownable {
  address public owner;
  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }
  modifier onlyOwner() { require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function"); _; }
}

// Pausable inherits Ownable
contract Pausable is Ownable {
  bool public paused = false;
  modifier whenNotPaused() { require(!paused, "Contract is paused"); _; }
  function pause() public onlyOwner whenNotPaused { paused = true; }
  function unpause() public onlyOwner { paused = false; }
}

// MyToken inherits Pausable
contract MyToken is Pausable {
  mapping(address => uint256) public balances;
  function transfer(address recipient, uint256 amount) public whenNotPaused returns (bool) { /* ... */ }
}
Checklist
  • Implement onlyOwner and transferOwnership safely.
  • Ensure whenNotPaused prevents transfers while paused.
  • Test pause/unpause and validate transfer behavior in both states.
Scenario
If deployer pauses the contract before a token sale, all transfers must revert until unpause is called by the owner.
Key Takeaway

Compose simple, audited base contracts for cross-cutting concerns and test their interactions thoroughly.

screens.title: Common pitfalls & best practices
screens.narratorSegment: There are several recurrent pitfalls when using inheritance in Solidity that can cause compilation errors or subtle runtime surprises. First, forgetting virtual on a base function prevents intended overriding and will block further specialization. Second, omitting override on a derived function that attempts to change a base implementation results in a compiler error — Solidity requires explicit intent. Third, failing to list all parent contracts in override(A, B) when overriding a function present in multiple bases also causes an error. Beyond compiler details, overly deep or diamond-shaped inheritance hierarchies increase the difficulty of reasoning and auditing; keep inheritance shallow and explicit. Rely on composition where appropriate: sometimes composing small helper contracts as libraries or using interfaces for external integrations reduces complexity. Another best practice is to mark only intended extension points as virtual rather than making every function virtual by default. Write unit tests that exercise expected override chains and use small, focused contracts for cross-cutting concerns like ownership and pausability. Lastly, document the inheritance order and the intended behavior when super is invoked so maintainers and auditors can quickly trace the method resolution and side effects. These practices reduce risk in deployed contracts where bugs are costly.

Core Concept
Pitfalls & Best Practices
  • Missing virtual prevents overrides; missing override causes compile errors.
  • When overriding functions from multiple bases, list all parent names in override(...).
  • Prefer shallow hierarchies and composition to avoid audit complexity.
  • Document intended extension points and side effects when calling super.
Warning
Complex inheritance increases risk. Each additional base adds to reasoning cost when auditing behavior.
Practical checklist
Testing
Write unit tests that confirm which implementation runs for functions defined in multiple bases and test modifier interactions thoroughly.
Documentation
Document why functions are virtual and where override is expected so future maintainers understand extension points.

screens.title: Design patterns: when to inherit vs compose
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between inheritance and composition is a key design decision. Inheritance works well when multiple contracts share state or when you want a partial implementation that many derived contracts will reuse. Abstract contracts shine when you need shared helpers, default implementations, or common storage, while requiring certain functions to be implemented by children. Interfaces are ideal when you care only about external behavior and need a lightweight contract to enable interoperability. Composition—using libraries or storing references to other contracts that expose an interface—is preferable when you want to minimize coupling and make behavior replaceable at runtime. For example, if you want interchangeable payment processors, define a payment interface and store the processor address in a separate manager contract; replaceability is easy without inheritance complexity. A common misconception is that inheritance is always simpler; in fact, deep inheritance often obfuscates the code path. As a rule, prefer small focused base contracts for cross-cutting concerns and use interfaces to define external APIs. When you choose inheritance, make extension points explicit with virtual and clearly document the linearization order to reduce surprises during audits and upgrades.

keyIdea.text: Use inheritance for shared state and default logic; prefer interfaces and composition for replaceable or external APIs to reduce coupling.

Architecture
Inherit when you need shared state
Abstract contracts provide shared helpers and storage. Use them when derived contracts should share an internal representation or logic.
Example
Ownable defines owner state and onlyOwner modifier used by many derived contracts.
Compose when you need replaceability
Interfaces and composition let you swap implementations without deep inheritance changes, ideal for external integrations and upgradeable components.
Example
Store a processor address conforming to a payment interface so you can replace processors without changing the consumer contract.
Practice prompt
For a feature that may change often, prefer composition + interface. For shared state and invariants, prefer inheritance.

screens.title: Testing and security considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance decisions directly impact how easy it is to test and audit contracts. When you centralize logic in base contracts, a single audit can cover shared behavior, but bugs in a base affect all derived contracts. Always write unit tests for both the base’s default behavior and the derived contract’s overrides; include tests that assert modifier interactions, event emissions, and that super chains run as expected. For multiple inheritance, include tests that verify the chosen implementation is called for colliding functions and that combined side effects match intentions. From a security perspective, prefer explicit overrides and avoid leaving important checks implicit in a deep inheritance chain. When you deploy, make sure constructor parameters and ownership are set as intended — mis-initialized state in a base constructor can be difficult to remediate after deployment. Also document and limit which functions are virtual to reduce an attacker’s surface when code is reused. Finally, keep inheritance hierarchies small and supplement with interfaces or composition when you need replaceability or external integration; smaller, focused contracts are easier to reason about and less likely to hide unintended behavior during an audit.

Test base and derived contracts thoroughly
Write unit tests for default base behavior, derived overrides, and modifier interactions. Confirm that events and state changes occur in the expected order when super is called.

Ensure base constructors initialize state correctly and ownership is assigned to the intended account.

Limit virtual functions and document intended overrides to aid auditors in tracing behavior.

Testing and explicitness mitigate the main risks introduced by inheritance choices in Solidity.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the concise concepts to carry forward. Inheritance lets a derived contract reuse public and internal members from a base contract, reducing duplication. Keep these points in mind when designing contracts: limit virtual functions, prefer shallow hierarchies, and test override chains to reduce surprises during audits and deployment. In this chapter you will learn how Solidity uses inheritance to make smart contracts modular, reusable, and easier to audit. We begin by defining what it means for one contract to inherit another, how derived contracts gain access to public and internal members, and why that matters when you build shared infrastructure like ownership, pausability, or payment logic. You will see the explicit rules Solidity enforces with the virtual and override keywords to avoid accidental behavior changes, and we will step through abstract contracts and interfaces to understand when to provide a partial implementation versus only a function signature. We will also examine multiple inheritance and Solidity’s method resolution order, so you can predict which implementation is chosen when multiple base contracts define the same function. Throughout the chapter you will follow concrete code examples: a payment gateway extended by a subscription gateway and a small token built from Ownable and Pausable bases. By the end, you will be able to design clean base contracts, avoid common compilation errors, and choose between abstract contracts and interfaces with confidence. Consider when a shared behavior should be a base contract rather than copied into every contract — that choice affects readability and security.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when building and auditing Solidity contracts. First, you will understand and apply Solidity's inheritance syntax and mechanics to create modular, reusable contracts that reduce duplication and clarify intent. Second, you will learn to use the virtual and override keywords correctly — an explicit requirement in Solidity — so you can intentionally modify base behavior and avoid compile-time errors. Third, you will be able to design abstract contracts and interfaces: decide when to provide partial implementations and when to declare only signatures for interoperability. Fourth, you will explain how multiple inheritance is resolved through C3 Linearization, so you can predict which base implementation takes precedence and avoid surprising behavior. Each objective pairs a conceptual understanding with a competency milestone: build a small derived contract, modify a virtual function, implement an abstract function, and reason about ordering in a multi-base scenario. These skills will make your smart contracts easier to maintain and safer to extend. Keep an eye out for common pitfalls: missing virtual keywords, incorrect override lists, and overly deep inheritance hierarchies that complicate audits.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical application and avoiding common pitfalls. You will learn to design contracts with clear ownership and modifiers so access control is reusable across derived contracts. You will practice implementing abstract functions and interfaces so concrete contracts satisfy required signatures and can interoperate with external systems. You will also learn to spot and rectify mistakes: missing virtual on base functions prevents safe overriding, missing override in a derived contract causes compilation errors, and complex multi-level inheritance chains make audits harder. Finally, you will know how to structure a hands-on activity: build an Ownable base, a Pausable base that inherits Ownable, and then a MyToken contract that composes both. This exercise reinforces modifier usage, state sharing, and transfer restrictions while paused. Each objective links a concept to a small milestone so you can test your work, for example by compiling with and without virtual or override to observe the compiler errors and by writing simple unit tests to confirm that when paused, transfers revert. This practice reduces deployment risk and makes behavior explicit.

Inheritance in Solidity is the mechanism by which one contract acquires the state variables and functions of another, enabling reuse and modular design. A contract that inherits is called the derived or child contract, and the contract being inherited from is the base or parent. When you declare contract Child is Parent, Child gains access to Parent’s public and internal members, which means you do not need to repeat common code like ownership checks, utility functions, or shared storage. A practical example is an Ownable base contract that stores the owner address and provides an onlyOwner modifier; derived contracts can use the modifier to protect sensitive functions without reimplementing the ownership check. One important detail is visibility: private members are not inherited, while internal and public are. Internal is useful for helper functions that should be visible to children but not exposed externally. Another nuance is constructors: if your base contract has initialization logic, derived contracts must ensure the base constructor is invoked either implicitly or via explicit parameters in the derived constructor. A common misconception is assuming inheritance copies code at deploy time; instead, the derived contract’s bytecode includes the selected behaviors, and explicit overrides determine which implementation is active. Think of inheritance as a design-time composition tool to centralize logic and make auditing easier when used with clear boundaries.

The virtual and override keywords are Solidity’s explicit contract between base and derived contracts. Declaring a base function as virtual indicates that you intend it to be customizable by children. A derived contract that changes that function must mark its implementation with override. This pair enforces clarity: the compiler refuses accidental overrides and requires you to express intent. When multiple base contracts define the same signature, the derived override must list all affected bases in override(...). For example, if A and B both provide foo, and C inherits A and B, then a new implementation in C must include override(A, B) to compile. A common workflow is: mark base hooks that are intended to be specialized as virtual, implement default behavior in the base, then override in derived contracts and optionally call super to retain base logic. Using super. functionName lets you extend behavior rather than fully replace it. An example is a payment function that emits a log in the base and allows derived contracts to perform validations before calling super to preserve the event emission. A frequent pitfall is forgetting to mark the base function virtual; the compiler then prevents any derived override. Explicitness reduces surprise in deployed contracts where unintentional overrides could cause serious issues.

Calling the parent's implementation from an overriding function is a common pattern when you want to add checks or state updates while keeping base behavior intact. In Solidity you call super. functionName to invoke the next implementation in the inheritance chain as resolved by the compiler. A typical case is PaymentGateway with a processPayment function that emits an event and returns true. A SubscriptionPaymentGateway overrides processPayment to validate a subscription amount and then calls super. processPayment to retain the original emission and any shared accounting logic. This pattern reduces code duplication and ensures shared side effects, like event emission or bookkeeping, remain consistent across implementations. However, be mindful when multiple inheritance is present: super resolves according to C3 Linearization, so the exact parent invoked depends on the inheritance order. Another practical detail is ordering of side effects: perform validation first, then call super if validation passes, or call super first if you must perform a base action before derived behavior, but be explicit. A misconception is assuming super always calls the immediate parent; in multiple inheritance, super walks the linearized chain. When you rely on super, document why you call it and test the combined behavior thoroughly to avoid subtle surprises.

Abstract contracts and interfaces both enforce structure but serve different design goals. An abstract contract can include implemented functions, state variables, and unimplemented functions marked as abstract; it cannot be deployed until its abstract functions are implemented by a derived contract. Use abstract contracts when you want to provide shared behavior or state but still force certain functions to be implemented by children. For example, an abstract PaymentProcessor might define a processPayment function signature without implementation while providing utility helpers to manage recipients. Interfaces are stricter: declared with the interface keyword, they contain only function signatures, cannot declare state or constructors, and are used to define public APIs that many contracts can adhere to. Choose an interface when you need a minimal, language-level guarantee about external calls and when you expect third-party contracts to implement the same signatures. A useful pattern is to code against interfaces for external interactions and inherit from abstract contracts for internal shared logic. A common misconception is thinking interfaces and abstract contracts are interchangeable; in practice interfaces are for external contracts and type checking, while abstract contracts are for partial implementations that supply shared code. Decide based on whether you need shared storage or only a signature contract.

Solidity supports multiple inheritance, which is powerful but demands discipline. When a contract inherits from multiple base contracts that define the same function signature, Solidity resolves which implementation is used using C3 Linearization, also described as method resolution order. The rule of thumb for Solidity is that the rightmost base in the is list has priority unless the derived contract explicitly overrides the function. For example, contract C is A, B will prefer B’s implementation of foo if both A and B implement it. If you need a different resolution or want to combine behavior, declare an override in C and call super to chain into the linearized sequence. A common mistake is assuming leftmost bases take precedence; developers should instead inspect the is ordering and add explicit override declarations to make intent clear. Very deep or diamond-shaped hierarchies make reasoning hard and increase audit surface area. Best practice is to keep the hierarchy shallow, document the expected linearization, and write unit tests that confirm which implementation runs for ambiguous functions. Also prefer explicit overrides that list parent contracts when you want to be very clear about which base implementations you are changing.
